Neighborhoods, terrain, and lots
Source-linked reconstruction (2026-11-26). The original lesson file was not found in the recovered archives. This new lesson describes the actual current host and recognizer, rather than claiming to be the missing original.

A neighborhood is the set of nearby units or cells that a unit can sense. Membership can change as units move. The trained morphogen recognizer uses local neighborhoods, sensed features, and a radius-dependent model to classify each unit's formation. It does not require each unit to know the entire world. Preserve unit identity when the neighborhood changes.

Terrain is the environment's state and constraints. In the existing hostworld.js, the host has a two-dimensional grid, ground row, sky, temperature, clock, particles, passages, and systems. The host exposes observable state rather than a predetermined swarm solution. Boundary cells and closed passages can block movement. The existing GameEngineHost makes a passage in the native world and associates it with a simulator; a learned interaction must satisfy the host's reach condition and change the observed passage state.

A lot is a proposed subdivision of terrain with its own extent, access constraints, occupancy and intended use. Lots are not a native hostworld.js class. Treat them as a design task: represent their boundaries as explicit cells or coordinates and expose permitted actions. Avoid silently changing the underlying host or treating a lot label as proof of accessibility.

Exercise: create two neighborhoods separated by a closed passage, move a unit near the passage, observe the failed crossing, demonstrate an allowed interaction, and verify that the passage becomes traversable. Then test the learned behavior against a different passage. Store the outcome and the original unit identity. A second exercise partitions an empty grid into candidate lots, verifies non-overlap and reachable access, and retains a successful formation only after the host checks pass.

Sources: vendor/synthia-swarm/hostworld.js; gameenginex_host.js; gameenginex_morph.js; organism_swarm.js; codex3/morphogen-swarm-lab/swarm.js and trained-models.js. The lot exercise is a proposal, not a claim of already implemented lot tooling.
